newsitem.title: USA: OPTIONS- FX vols off highs as spot takes breather.
newsitem.headline: OPTIONS- FX vols off highs as spot takes breather.

text.p: Implied volatilities for dollar-pair options were slightly off early highs in afternoon U.S. trade as a rebound in the spot greenback stalled short of Monday's peaks, dealers said.
Still, Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's comments supported the dollar, underpinning volatilities, as they were perceived to be generally friendly to U.S. asset markets, traders said.
"As long as the dollar is testing highs, you just can't sell off volatilities," said Kyoko Hiramatsu, senior dealer at Bank of Yokohama in New York.
"Profit-taking seems to have picked up somewhat in New York time, though," she added.
One-month dollar/mark implied volatility stood at 9.1/9.3 percent, off about 0.2 point from early highs and little changed from Monday.

Risk reversals, which reflect pricing differential between puts and calls, continued to show good bid for mark puts. One-month 25-delta was at about 0.3/0.6 percent in favor of mark puts, while one-year was around par.
One-month dollar/yen implied volatility was off a touch at 8.95/9.15 percent.
Traders said the dollar must break above 118 yen decisively and break above Monday's 118.29 yen high to spark a fresh round of volatility bids.
One-month 25-delta risk-reversal stood at 0.0/0.2 percent bid for yen puts. From about three-months and out, risk reversals were flat or slightly bid for yen calls.

After modest pullbacks in the spot dollar early in the day, Greenspan's testimony to the Senate Budget Committeee buoyed U.S. stock and bond markets and pushed the dollar back up to around 1.6270 marks and 118.00 yen.

"If you look at the long bonds, they were down in anticipation of some further loose-lip Greenspan comment on 'irrational exuberance' or high wage growth or something," a trader at a U.S. bank in California said.
"However, the comments proved to be very benign and bonds have subsequently recovered and it looks the dollar is just holding steady at these levels," he added.
Greenspan did express concerns over wage increases and described the stock market's rise as "breathtaking," but traders said markets appeared to have had priced-in stronger language.
Earlier, Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin's comment that a strong dollar was in the United States' self-interest also supported the greenback.

Elsewhere, sterling volatilities stayed firm on beliefs that a recent dip in spot could have run its course. Traders said the pound's long-term bullish trend was still intact due partly to lingering speculation of an interest rate hike.
One-month cable volatility was slightly firmer at 8.7/8.9 percent.
